standard.title: Interpret music
standard.description: interpret music in a variety of forms and/or styles, manipulating elements of music and employing relevant vocal/instrumental techniques
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can manipulate elements of music and use compositional devices to communicate ideas when composing and practising music for performance (AC9AMU6C01). They can notate, document and/or record music they compose. They have not yet focused on interpretation of existing works across a variety of forms and styles, nor on deliberately employing style-specific vocal/instrumental techniques to realise stylistic features.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students interpret music in a variety of forms and/or styles by manipulating elements of music and employing relevant vocal/instrumental techniques to realise stylistic features and achieve intended expressive effects.

nodes.label: Identifying stylistic features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the stylistic features of a piece of music that need to be realised in performance, including relevant elements of music and technical demands
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two stylistic features of a given piece and describe what they require from a performer
nodes.typical_width: Identify stylistic features across a range of forms/styles; describe what each requires technically and expressively from the performer
wider: Analyse recordings of expert performers to identify how specific stylistic features are realised differently across interpretations of the same work
Compare stylistic features across two contrasting genres (e.g. jazz and classical) to identify what changes technically and what remains common

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of stylistic feature examples before they can reliably identify and target them in their own interpretation. Exposure to multiple styles and forms builds the reference bank that makes identification purposeful rather than guesswork.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two stylistic features of a piece
Describes what each feature requires from a performer (technical or expressive demand)

nodes.label: Trialling techniques for stylistic effect
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can trial and select vocal/instrumental techniques that realise identified stylistic features, including manipulation of dynamics, timbre, articulation and accent/stress
nodes.minimum_width: Trial at least one technique (e.g. accent placement, dynamic shaping, timbre manipulation) and explain how it contributes to the stylistic effect
nodes.typical_width: Trial multiple techniques across elements of music; compare approaches and select those that best realise the intended style; document choices as a reference
wider: Experiment with effects such as distortion, decay or delay to achieve stylistic feel in digital or amplified performance contexts; evaluate how these change the expressive character of the music

Investigate how the same melodic or rhythmic pattern sounds and feels differently when accent/stress placement is changed — connect this to genre-specific performance conventions (e.g. swing feel, syncopation in funk)

response_modes.reason: Students frequently apply techniques mechanically without understanding their stylistic purpose. Trialling the same technique across multiple contexts (acoustic vs digital, different genres) helps students hear what the technique does and why it matters — shifting from execution to interpretation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The digital effects direction (distortion, decay, delay) opens a genuinely distinct performance context — students who extend here are reasoning about timbre and style in contemporary production contexts, not just applying acoustic technique.
success_criteria: Trials at least one vocal/instrumental technique with a clear stylistic rationale
Can explain how the technique contributes to the intended stylistic effect

nodes.label: Rehearsing toward interpretation goals
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use student and teacher set goals to focus rehearsal, tracking progress toward an intended interpretation
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one explicit goal to focus rehearsal; identify whether the goal was met and what still needs work
nodes.typical_width: Set and use multiple rehearsal goals across technical and expressive dimensions; adjust goals as rehearsal progresses; document decisions
wider: Record alternative approaches to interpreting a phrase or melody and evaluate each against the intended stylistic effect — use the recording to identify what the ear notices that playing alone doesn't reveal
Limited width — rehearsal goal-setting is a process skill; breadth comes from the variety of repertoire and styles rehearsed, not from multiplying goal-setting procedures.

response_modes.reason: Goal-directed rehearsal is a precision and persistence skill — students need sustained practice with the feedback loop (set goal → rehearse → evaluate → adjust) rather than exposure to more contexts. The cognitive work is in the iteration, not the variety.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one explicit rehearsal goal
Can describe whether and how the goal was met

nodes.label: Working from notation and documentation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can interpret music notated or documented in a range of formats, using the notation as a basis for developing their interpretation
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one notation format (staff notation, tablature, chord chart, graphic score, or recording) to inform an interpretation
nodes.typical_width: Use multiple notation formats to develop an interpretation; identify what each format communicates and what it leaves open for interpretive decision-making
wider: Use a recording and a chart (melody, form, harmony/chords) to develop an arrangement of a song — make deliberate interpretive decisions about elements the chart leaves unspecified
Compare how the same piece looks and sounds when documented in two different formats (e.g. staff notation vs chord chart) and explain what each format prioritises for the performer

response_modes.reason: Students need familiarity with a range of notation formats to work fluently across genres and performance contexts. Accumulating experience with different formats — what each captures and what each leaves open — builds the practical literacy that interpretation depends on.

success_criteria: Uses at least one notation format to inform an interpretation
Makes at least one deliberate interpretive decision not fully specified by the notation

nodes.label: Integrated interpretation across a piece
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can produce an interpretation of a piece in a chosen style that integrates stylistic feature decisions, technique choices, notation reading and rehearsal goals into a coherent expressive whole
nodes.minimum_width: Perform or record an interpretation that realises at least two identified stylistic features using appropriate technique
nodes.typical_width: Perform or record an interpretation that demonstrates consistent stylistic understanding across the piece, with technique choices that support expressive intent throughout; reflect on what worked and what would change
wider: Compare two contrasting interpretations of the same piece (own and a recording) to evaluate how different technique choices realise the same stylistic features differently
Perform music in a variety of forms or styles across the unit, demonstrating that stylistic interpretation choices are style-specific rather than universal defaults

response_modes.reason: This is where stylistic identification, technique selection, notation reading and rehearsal goal-setting come together in a single performance. The coordination of these components is the learning — students discover that interpretation is not a sequence of separate decisions but a unified expressive act.

success_criteria: Produces an interpretation that realises at least two stylistic features
Technique choices are appropriate to the style and support expressive intent
